We worked with @thinkymachines to make Inkling 2 Mini run fast locally:

- 210 tok/sec decode, 3620 tok/sec prefill on 96GB M5 Ultra Mac Studio
- 125 tok/sec decode, 1750 tok/sec prefill on 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro

It built a native weather app 1.8x faster than Claude Sonnet 5.5 on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio and 11x cheaper (API pricing).

The looping architecture is ideal for local devices like MacBooks, which are memory constrained. Looping layers of the model increases inference-time compute (and intelligence) without increasing the size of the model.

quoted_tweet.author: ItsOkayStudio
quoted_tweet.text:
Incredible. Right now I’m thinking about  something that sometimes gets missed in the excitement around AI. 

In 1859, Riemann had no computers, No ability to examine trillions of zeros. No modern computational tools. He was working with mathematical structures that cannot be directly perceived by the senses.

And somehow, through abstraction, intuition, and mathematical reasoning, he identified a possible structural truth about an infinite mathematical landscape.

In other words, he proposed something about infinity using a finite human mind.

Now, 167 years later, we’re at the point where an AI, supported by an extraordinary accumulation of human mathematical knowledge, can establish that his intuition was correct.

That’s pure poetry.

We tend to frame advanced AI as evidence of how limited human intelligence is. But this would also demonstrate something astonishing about our intelligence: the human mind can sometimes recognize the architecture of a truth long before it possesses the means to prove it.

The machine may ultimately establish the proof. But it was a human who first saw where to look.

We should marvel at the intelligence capable of confirming such a truth. But we should be equally astonished by the intelligence that could conceive of it 167 years earlier.

That’s an extraordinary reason to be encouraged about our species.

And perhaps a reminder that our greatest intellectual achievement isn’t necessarily finding answers. Sometimes it’s our seemingly inexplicable ability to ask precisely the right question.
